property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any supplied _owner address, after calling setOwner(_owner) the contract's owner must equal the provided _owner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead breaks this by setting owner to the caller rather than the supplied _owner for some _owner inputs.

For every caller address x, when setOwner(...) is successfully called by the current owner, C.owner() becomes the provided _owner; the mutant instead clears owner to address(0) so this property is violated for inputs where _owner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) on the correct contract updates the public owner to _owner; the mutant that omits the assignment leaves owner unchanged, so this property is violated for inputs where _owner != original owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(target), the contract's owner public getter equals the provided target address after the call; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead can break this by making owner == tx.origin != target when the call is proxied (msg.sender != tx.origin).

If a current owner calls setOwner(via) to set owner to a target address, then after the call the contract's owner must equal the provided target; the mutant that assigns owner = tx.origin will break this when msg.sender != tx.origin (i.e., when the call is proxied through a contract), because owner becomes the external tx.origin instead of the provided target.

For any proxy contract address P (fuzzed) that the current owner uses to call setOwner(target), when the call succeeds the reference sets owner to the provided target address, but the mutant that assigns owner = tx.origin will instead set owner to the original transaction origin (not the provided target) when msg.sender != tx.origin—so owner == target for all admissible inputs in the reference, and some proxied inputs will break the mutant.

For any caller that is the immediate msg.sender (including contracts) the correct contract sets owner to the provided _owner after a successful setOwner call; the mutant that assigns owner = tx.origin will break this when the call is proxied through an intermediate contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) because owner becomes tx.origin instead of the provided _owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address _owner, after calling setOwner(_owner) the contract's public owner getter equals the provided _owner; the mutant that assigns owner = tx.origin breaks this when the owner call is proxied through another contract (msg.sender != tx.origin), causing owner to become tx.origin instead of the provided _owner.

For all callers, calling setOwner(x) from the current owner updates the public owner variable to x; the mutant requiring msg.sender == address(0) prevents legitimate owners from changing owner, so for some caller-address inputs the mutant leaves owner unchanged while the reference updates it.

Invariant: only the current owner can successfully call setOwner(address) to change owner; the mutant allowing non-owners breaks this by permitting some non-owner address to successfully change owner.
For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) completes and returns true (reference); the mutant changes the return to false for some valid owner calls, breaking this rule.

For every caller who is the owner, calling setOwner(_owner) completes (does not revert) and returns true while updating the public owner to _owner; the mutant sometimes returns false even though it still updates owner, violating the rule that setOwner called by the owner always returns true on success.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) succeeds (does not revert) and returns true — the mutant sometimes returns false despite succeeding, breaking this rule.

For every caller equal to the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) completes successfully and returns true; the mutant still updates owner but can return false, violating this return-value rule.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(newOwner) on the correct contract always updates the public owner to newOwner; the mutant clears owner and returns early so some owner calls leave owner set to address(0) instead of newOwner.

For any caller address X and newOwner Y, when X is the current owner the reference contract always allows setOwner(Y) to succeed (owner becomes Y); the mutant that additionally requires tx.origin == owner prevents calls that originate from a different tx.origin even if msg.sender == owner (e.g., when owner is a contract), thus breaking this rule for some inputs.
For every caller and input, only the current owner can successfully change C.owner via setOwner; the mutant removing the require allows some non-owner caller to change owner, violating this rule.
